name: Jonathan Cazabonne
role: Ph.D. candidate at the Institut de recherche sur les forêts (Université du Québec en Abitibi-Témiscamingue), studying fungal diversity and its interactions with other kingdoms — with a focus on ectomycorrhizal symbioses and fungus–arthropod associations — to help bring fungi into biodiversity conservation and sustainable forest management.
bio: I hold a B.Sc. in organismal, population and ecosystem biology and an M.Sc. in forest ecology and management, and I'm now a Ph.D. candidate at the Institut de recherche sur les forêts (UQAT), supervised by Maxence Martin and Mélanie Roy. My research aims for a finer understanding of fungal diversity — morphological and genetic — and of fungal interactions with other kingdoms, approached through molecular ecology, community ecology, integrative taxonomy, citizen science, and even literature and art. My doctoral work focuses on soil fungal communities in the old-growth boreal forests of eastern Canada: their diversity, their ecological functions (especially in the forest carbon cycle), and how new tools such as airborne LiDAR and the Potential Biodiversity Index could help monitor fungal diversity within ecosystem-based forest management. I'm also a member of #TeamLaboul, a research group studying the diversity and conservation of Laboulbeniomycetes — a group of fungi strictly associated with arthropods — and of "Réécrire la forêt boréale," a cross-institutional project exploring the literary potential of scientific research on fungi. Across all of this, my goal is twofold: help integrate fungi into biodiversity conservation and ecosystem-based forest management, and bring fungi to public attention. I also edit the Sydowia Fungal Systematic and Evolution (FUSE) series and co-edited a Fungal Ecology special issue, "Fungal conservation: from knowledge to actions."
